Students will also be expected to determine the benefits and drawbacks of computational thinking within given problem scenarios, justifying their choices based on the context and requirements of the task. For 1.1.4 students will need to know different computational thinking methods that can be used to solve problems, including: • Decomposition (links with 1.1.6 to 1.1.10) • Pattern recognition (links with 1.1.11 and 1.1.12) • Abstraction (links with 1.1.13 to 1.1.16) • Algorithmic design (links with 1.2) For each computational thinking method, students will need to: • Understand its definition and purpose • Recognise where it can be used in given problems • Apply the method to given problems For 1.1.5 students will need to understand the benefits and drawbacks of each computational thinking method listed in 1.1.4. They will be expected to identify and explain these benefits and drawbacks when solving problems. Additionally, students will need to evaluate each method within given problem scenarios, justifying their choices based on the specific context and requirements of the task. For 1.1.6 students will need to understand the purpose of decomposition and how this can be used when solving problems. For 1.1.7 students will need to understand the key tasks involved in decomposition, including: • Identifying the main features of a problem • Clearly characterising each identified feature • Breaking problems down into smaller, more manageable parts • Breaking solutions down into smaller, more manageable parts For 1.1.8 students will need to be able to apply the decomposition tasks outlined in 1.1.7 within given problem scenarios. For 1.1.9 students will need to understand different methods used to represent decomposition, including: • Block diagrams — Students will need to create diagrams using blocks to show the main components or modules of a software solution (complete or partial) and how these interact • Information flow diagrams — Students will need to illustrate how data moves through a software system or process, identifying inputs, outputs, and data transformations • Flowcharts — Students will need to produce step-by-step visual instructions of processes within a software solution, using the symbols stated in Appendix 2 of the specification to represent instructions, decisions and flow of control. Links with 1.2.2 and 1.2.3 • Code — Students will need to write Python programming code that break down a solution into manageable, reusable parts, demonstrating organisation of data and logic. Links with 1.2.2 and 1.2.5 • Written descriptions — Students will need to provide clear, structured explanations to represent how a problem or solution is broken down into smaller parts. Links with 1.2.2 and 1.2.4 Students will need to select the most appropriate representation method based on the problem context and recognise the purpose and features of each representation method. Links with 1.2.2. For 1.1.10 students will need to be able to apply the decomposition representation methods stated in 1.1.9 to clearly represent the breakdown of given problem scenarios. For 1.1.11 students will need to understand the purpose of pattern recognition and how this can be used when solving problems. For 1.1.12 students will need to apply different methods of pattern recognition in given problem scenarios by: • Identifying and interpreting trends and similarities within and across problems and processes • Recognising common features between a new problem and existing solutions • Making predictions and assumptions based on the patterns they observe For 1.1.13 students will need to understand the purpose of abstraction and how this can be used when solving problems. For 1.1.14 students will need to understand the key tasks involved in abstraction, including: • Identifying the essential information that is needed in order to solve a problem • Filtering out unnecessary or irrelevant details that are not needed to solve a problem • Hiding the internal workings or complexity that are not important to the overall solution An example of how 1.1.14 could be assessed in core exam paper 1 is shown here: For 1.1.15 students will need to apply different methods of abstraction in given problem scenarios by: • Identifying the inputs required for the solution, such as the data or information needed to start the process • Defining the expected outputs and outcomes, including what results the solution should produce • Recognising elements that will vary between different uses or instances of the solution • Recognising elements that will remain constant and do not change during the process • Determining the key actions the solution must perform to achieve its objectives • Identifying repeated processes or tasks that the solution will carry out multiple times For 1.1.16 students will need to be able to apply abstraction to given problem scenarios by using the tasks outlined in 1.1.15. For 1.1.17 students will need to understand how the components of different computational thinking (decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and algorithmic design) relate and work together. They will need to make judgements about when and how to use each component effectively in digital software development. They will also need to determine the suitability of applying specific components or combinations of components to different problem-solving scenarios. Content area 1.2 (Algorithmic design) For 1.2.1 students will need to understand the definition of the term ‘algorithm’ and recognise its key characteristics, such as the need for precision and finiteness. They will also need to understand the purpose of algorithms in problem solving. For 1.2.2 students will need to understand that algorithms can be expressed in different formats, including flowcharts, written descriptions, and Python code. They will need to recognise and understand: • The components of flowcharts, such as terminators, processes, sub- processes, decisions, inputs/outputs, arrows, and labels, using the symbols outlined in Appendix 2 of the specification • How written descriptions use hierarchical markers to show the sequence of steps in an algorithm • That algorithms can be represented in Python code using specific Python commands as outlined in Appendix 2 of the specification For 1.2.3 to 1.2.5 students will need to understand the benefits and drawbacks of using flowcharts, written descriptions, and Python code when writing algorithms to solve problems and in given problem scenarios. An example of how 1.2.3 could be assessed in core exam paper 1 is shown here: For 1.2.6 students will need to understand that the order of an algorithm is crucial to ensure it functions correctly. They will need to know the meanings of the terms sequence, selection, and iteration, and how these concepts can be used to represent the order in which an algorithm is executed. Students will also need to know how to represent sequence, selection and iteration in the different algorithm notations stated in 1.2.2. For 1.2.7 students will need to understand what an algorithm is and its overall purpose. They will need to be able to explain how a given algorithm works step- by-step and identify the problem it is designed to solve. Additionally, students will need to analyse an algorithm to describe its intended outcome or result. For 1.2.8 students will need to understand how inputs are processed by an algorithm and be able to apply the algorithm step-by-step to given inputs in order to find the output. They will need to trace the logic of an algorithm to predict the correct output and work with different types of input data to determine the resulting output. For 1.2.9 students will need to analyse an algorithm to spot logic errors that affect its correctness or efficiency. They will also need to apply problem-solving skills to locate where an algorithm does not perform as expected. For 1.2.10 students will need to know how to make possible corrections or improvements to fix identified errors in an algorithm. For 1.2.11 students will be expected to transfer between the different algorithm notations stated in 1.2.2. They will need to be able to convert algorithms presented in one notation—such as flowcharts, written descriptions, or Python code—into another. For example, students should be able to convert a given flowchart into Python code or vice versa. For 1.2.12 students will need to understand what actions are within the context of algorithms, such as steps that perform specific tasks or operations. They will need to design algorithms that incorporate clear and logical sequences of these actions and create solutions where actions are used to manipulate data or control the flow of the algorithm. Additionally, students will need to apply problem-solving skills to develop algorithms that effectively use actions to achieve the desired outcomes. An example of how 1.2.12 could be assessed in core exam paper 1 is shown here: An example of how 1.2.12 could be assessed in the Employer Set Project (Task 3) is shown here: Content area 1.3 (Strategies) For 1.3.1 students will need to understand the different approaches to solving problems, including: • Top-down • Bottom-up • Modularisation They will need to understand the purpose of each approach and when it is appropriate to use them. Students will also need to be able to explain the differences between the top- down, bottom-up, and modularisation problem-solving methods. Additionally, they should be able to apply their knowledge to identify which approach would be most suitable in given problem scenarios. An example of how 1.3.1 could be assessed in core exam paper 1 is shown here: For 1.3.2 students will need to understand the benefits and drawbacks of the different approaches given in 1.3.1. They will need to be able to compare and contrast these benefits and drawbacks effectively. Students should apply this understanding to determine which approach is most effective for specific problem contexts. For 1.3.3 students will need to understand the purpose of root cause analysis in problem-solving and know when it should be applied. They will also need to be able to explain how root cause analysis helps identify the underlying causes of problems. For 1.3.4 students will need to know and understand different approaches to root cause analysis, including: • The five whys • Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) • Event Tree Analysis (ETA) They will need to understand how each root cause analysis method works and when it is appropriate to use them. Students will also need to know the actions to take after completing root cause analysis, such as: • Logging the findings • Closing the issue • Escalating it to an appropriate manager, specialist, or external third party when necessary An example of how 1.3.4 could be assessed in core exam paper 1 is shown here: For 1.3.5 students will need to know and understand each stage of the high- level problem-solving strategy: • Define the problem • Gather information • Analyse the information • Make a plan of action • Implement a solution • Review the solution They will need to understand the purpose of each stage in the problem-solving process. For 1.3.6 students will need to understand how different problems and the problem-solving strategies are interrelated. They will need to make judgements about the suitability of various problem-solving strategies for specific problems encountered in digital software development. Content Area 2 – Introduction to programming Students need to be able to analyse digital software development problems that may involve software, people, processes, and data. They need to use a variety of tools and techniques when developing a complete solution or a sub- part of a solution. Content area 2.1 (Standard Data Types) For 2.1.1 students will need to understand the definition of common data types, including • Integer • Float • String • Boolean Students will need to understand the purpose of each data type and when it is appropriate to use them in programming. Students will need to be able to identify examples of integer, float, string, and Boolean values within Python code or data. Students will need to apply their knowledge of these data types to select the correct type for variables when solving problems. This specification point contains links with Content Area 6.4 (Data Types). Content area 2.2 (Variables and Constants) For 2.2.1 and 2.2.2 students will need to understand the definition of variables and constants in programming. Students will need to understand the purpose of variables and constants as containers for storing data values. Students will need to understand when and why variables and constants are used within a program. For 2.2.3 students will need to understand the purpose of data type conversion functions in Python. Students will need to understand why data type conversion is necessary, such as to enable operations between different data types. Students will need to know the common data type conversion functions stated in Appendix 2 of the specification. For 2.2.4 students will need to understand the definition of scope in programming. Students will need to understand the role of scope in determining where variables and constants can be accessed within a program. Students will need to understand when and why scope is important in program design and debugging. For 2.2.5 students will need to understand the difference between global and local variables. Students will need to understand how global variables can be accessed throughout the entire program. Students also will need to understand how local variables are restricted to the block or function in which they are declared. An example of how 2.2.5 could be assessed in core exam paper 1 is shown here: For 2.2.6 students will need to apply their understanding of scope by declaring and using variables with appropriate scope in their programs. Students will need to use local variables within functions or blocks to limit variable accessibility. Students will need to use global variables only when necessary and understand the implications for program behaviour. For 2.2.7 students will need to apply their knowledge by declaring variables and constants using the common data types listed in 2.1.1. Students will need to use correct Python syntax to declare and initialise variables and constants. For 2.2.8 students will need to apply their knowledge by using variables to store and manipulate data in Python programs. Students will need to use constants appropriately to represent fixed values throughout their Python code. Students will need to demonstrate the ability to update variable values and reference constants correctly in Python programs. For 2.2.9 students will need to apply data type conversion functions in Python as indicated in Appendix 2 of the specification. Students will need to use these functions to ensure data compatibility during operations or input/output handling. Content area 2.3 (Data Structures) For 2.3.1 students will need to understand the standard data structures: list, array, and dictionary. Students will need to understand the purpose of each data structure and when to use a list, an array, or a dictionary in different programming scenarios. Students will need to be able to explain the differences between lists, arrays, and dictionaries. For 2.3.2 students will need to be able to read and interpret code that uses the data stated in 2.3.1. Students will need to understand how data is stored and accessed within these data structures in code. Students will need to trace the flow of data and predict the output when data structures are manipulated in code. For 2.3.3 students will need to apply their knowledge to write Python code that correctly implements the data structures listed in 2.3.1. Students will need to create programs that store, access, and manipulate data within these structures. Students will need to select the most appropriate data structure for a given problem when developing code. For 2.3.4 students will need to identify errors related to the use of data structures in code. Students will need to use debugging techniques to locate issues in how data structures are implemented or manipulated. Students will need to correct code to ensure data structures function as intended. Students will need to test and verify that fixes resolve the problems within the data structures. Content area 2.4 (Operators) For 2.4.1 students will need to understand the purpose and function of common arithmetic operators, including addition, subtraction, division, multiplication, exponentiation, integer division and modulus. For 2.4.2 students will need to understand the purpose of relational operators, including equivalence, less than, greater than, not equal, less than or equal to and greater than or equal to. Students will need to recognise how these operators are used to compare values in programming. For 2.4.3 students will need to understand the purpose of Boolean operators (NOT, AND, OR). Students will need to recognise how these operators combine or invert Boolean values in programming. For 2.4.4 students will need to be able to use arithmetic operators correctly to perform calculations in code. Students will need to be able to use relational operators to compare values and make decisions in programs. Students will need to be able to use Boolean operators to combine or invert logical conditions effectively. Students will need to apply these operators in combination to solve programming problems and control program flow. For 2.4.5 students will need to read and understand code that uses arithmetic, relational, and Boolean operators. Students will need to trace how these operators affect the flow of the program and the output produced. Students will need to explain the role of operators within given code. For 2.4.6 students will need to write code that correctly uses arithmetic, relational, and Boolean operators. Students will need to apply these operators to perform calculations, comparisons, and logical operations in programming tasks. Students will need to combine different operators to build effective program logic. For 2.4.7 students will need to identify errors related to the incorrect use of arithmetic, relational, or Boolean operators. Students will need to use debugging techniques to locate and fix issues in code involving these operators. Students will need to test corrected code to ensure the operators function as intended. Content area 2.5 (Input and Output) For 2.5.1 students will need to understand how input and output are implemented using different methods, including how to receive input from a keyboard and display output on a screen. They will also need to understand how to read from and write to text files. Furthermore, students will need to apply techniques to implement input and output operations using keyboards, screens, and text files effectively in their Python code. For 2.5.2 students will need to understand the purpose and use of text files for input and output, including how to open a text file for reading and writing data. They will need to be able to write lines of text to a file and understand the importance of closing a file after operations are complete. For 2.5.3 students will need to understand how input and output are used within code and be able to read and interpret code that involves input from devices or files. They will also need to interpret code that produces output to the screen or files. Furthermore, students will need to apply their knowledge to explain the flow of data through input and output operations in given code. For 2.5.4 students will need to be able to create code that correctly implements input and output operations. For 2.5.5 students will need to be able to identify errors related to input and output in code and use debugging methods to locate and fix issues with these operations. Content area 2.6 (Actions) For 2.6.1 students will need to understand what sequence means in programming, including its purpose in controlling the order of instructions. They will also need to recognise when sequence is used within a program’s flow. For 2.6.2 students will need to understand the concept of selection in programming and its purpose for making decisions within code. They will need to know when to use selection structures in a program and understand how different selection statements work, including: • if… • else… if… • else… • match/case For 2.6.3 students will need to understand the concept of loops in programming and their purpose for repeating actions in code. They will need to know when loops should be used to improve program efficiency and understand the difference between count-controlled loops and condition- controlled loops. For 2.6.4 students will need to know how count-controlled ‘for’ loops operate to repeat code a set number of times, as well as how condition-controlled ‘while do’ loops operate to repeat code based on a condition. An example of how 2.6.4 could be assessed in core exam paper 1 is shown here: For 2.6.5 students will need to understand the benefits and drawbacks of using loops in program code. Students will need to determine when loops are appropriate to use and when alternative structures might be better. For 2.6.6 students will need to understand how actions such as sequence, selection, and iteration are represented in code. They will need to be able to read and interpret code that uses sequence to control the order of instructions, selection statements to make decisions, and iteration to repeat actions. Additionally, students will need to apply their knowledge to explain how these actions affect program flow in given code. For 2.6.7 students will need to be able to develop Python code that correctly implements sequence, selection statements (if, else if, else, match/case) and iteration to repeat actions, including both count-controlled and condition- controlled loops. For 2.6.8 students will need to be able to identify errors related to sequence, selection, and iteration in code. They will need to use debugging techniques to locate issues affecting the flow of actions and correct errors involving the order of instructions, decision-making structures, and loops. Content area 2.7 (Functions and Procedures) For 2.7.1 students will need to understand the characteristics of functions in programming, including their purpose for organising and reusing code. They will need to know that functions may or may not take parameters as input and that they must return a result after execution. For 2.7.2 students will need to understand the characteristics of procedures in programming, including their purpose for organising code that performs tasks. They will need to know that procedures may or may not take parameters as input and that they must not return a result. For 2.7.3 students will need to understand the different sources of functions and procedures, such as: • User-written • Pre-written and built-in as part of the programming language • Pre-written and supplied in libraries as part of the programming language • Pre-written and supplied in libraries from third parties For 2.7.4 students will need to understand the benefits of using pre-written code when producing programs. For 2.7.5 students will need to understand how user-written functions and procedures are structured and used in code, as well as how pre-written functions and procedures are called and integrated within programs. They will need to be able to read and interpret code that uses both user-written and pre- written functions, and similarly interpret code that uses both user-written and pre-written procedures. For 2.7.6 students will need to be able to develop code that includes user- written functions to perform specific tasks, both with and without parameters. They will also need to create user-written procedures to organise code without returning a result, using parameters or no parameters. Additionally, students will need to incorporate pre-written functions from programming languages or libraries into their code and use pre-written procedures effectively within their programs. For 2.7.7 students will need to understand how to identify errors in code that uses both user-written and pre-written functions and procedures. They will need to apply debugging techniques to locate and fix problems in these user- written and pre-written components. Content area 2.8 (Validation) For 2.8.1 students will need to know the definition of validation and understand its purpose in ensuring that data is sensible and reasonable. They will need to know the purpose of different validation checks and when to use them, including • Presence – ensures that a value has been entered and is not left blank • Length – ensures that the data entered contains the correct number of characters • Range – ensures that numeric data falls within a specified minimum and maximum value • Type – ensures that the data entered is of the correct type (e.g., number, text, date) • Format – ensures that the data follows a specific pattern, such as a postcode or email address • Check digit – ensures that data, such as account numbers, is valid using an algorithm Students will not be expected to know any particular algorithm that is used to calculate a check digit For 2.8.2 students will need to understand how the validation checks listed in 2.8.1 are implemented in code and be able to identify the type of validation used. They will need to understand the purpose of each validation check within code and apply their knowledge to explain how validation determines whether input data is accepted or rejected. For 2.8.3 students will need to know how to write Python code to implement the validation checks listed in 2.8.1. Students will also need to select the most suitable validation methods for different types of input data and combine multiple validation checks where necessary to ensure data is sensible and reasonable. For 2.8.4 students will need to understand how to identify errors in code that uses validation checks. They will need to apply debugging techniques to find problems in the logic or implementation of validation and correct errors in different types of validation. Content area 2.9 (Design Considerations and Programming Practices) For 2.9.1 students will need to analyse a process to determine the correct and logical sequence of steps involved. For 2.9.2 students will need to understand the concept of order of operations in calculations and processes. They will also need to apply the correct order of operations to ensure that outputs are accurate and errors are avoided. For 2.9.3 students will need to evaluate different data structures in relation to specific problems or requirements. This includes assessing data structures based on their impact on execution time efficiency and how they affect memory usage. Students will need to determine the most appropriate data structure to use in order to optimise both execution time and memory efficiency. For 2.9.4 students will need to understand how the order of actions can affect both execution time and memory usage. They will need to analyse processes to identify the most efficient sequence of actions, determining the order that optimises execution time as well as the order that optimises memory usage. For 2.9.5 students will need to understand what naming conventions are and why they are important. They will need to recognise the purpose of using meaningful names in code, and understand the camelCase and snake_case conventions, including when to use each. For 2.9.6 students will need to understand how naming conventions affect code readability and recognise the role of white space in making code easier to read and understand. They will also need to understand why maintaining a maximum line length improves code clarity and evaluate how different code style conventions contribute to overall readability. For 2.9.7 students will need to assess an algorithm’s efficiency in terms of storage use and execution time and judge the appropriateness of the data structures chosen within it. They will also need to evaluate the suitability of data types, variables, and constants used in the algorithm, while considering the presentation and maintainability of the algorithm’s code. Students will need to make informed judgements about whether an algorithm meets the overall requirements effectively. Content area 2.10 (Robust Code) For 2.10.1 students will need to understand what robust code is and why it is important. They will need to recognise how robust code • Handles unexpected inputs • Handles unexpected terminations • Produces specific and meaningful error messages For 2.10.2 students will need to understand what debugging is and its purpose in software development. They will need to understand different types of errors in code, including syntax, logic, and runtime errors. Additionally, students will need to analyse and trace code in order to locate and correct these errors. For 2.10.3 students will need to understand how debugging contributes to creating robust solutions and recognise that it helps identify and fix errors that could cause failures. For 2.10.4 and 2.10.5 students will need to apply problem-solving skills to locate errors in given code and correct errors once found. Content area 2.11 (Common Algorithms) For 2.11.1 students will need to understand how both linear search and binary search algorithms operate, including the step-by-step process each one follows to locate a target value. Students will also need to know how to trace these algorithms with data provided. For 2.11.2 students will need to understand how bubble sort, insertion sort and merge sort operate, including the step-by-step process each follows to arrange data into a specified order. Students will also need to know how to trace these algorithms with data provided. An example of how 2.11.2 could be assessed in core exam paper 1 is shown here: For 2.11.3 students will need to understand the main advantages and disadvantages of each listed searching and sorting algorithm in 2.11.1 and 2.11.2. This includes factors such as speed, efficiency, memory use, ease of implementation, and suitability for different sizes or types of data sets. They should be able to compare the algorithms, explain why one may be preferred over another in a given situation, and recognise the trade-offs involved when selecting an algorithm for a specific task. Students will not be expected to make reference to Big-O notation. For 2.11.4 students will need to understand how algorithms can be evaluated and compared using key metrics, including: • The amount of memory space they require • Their execution time • The number of comparisons made during processing They should be able to explain what each metric measures, why it is important, and how it can affect the choice of algorithm. Students will also need to apply these metrics to compare different algorithms and justify which would be most suitable for a particular scenario. For 2.11.5 students will need to understand what is meant by the best case, worst case, and average case performance of an algorithm. They should be able to explain how these scenarios describe the conditions under which an algorithm performs most efficiently, least efficiently, and typically in practice. Students will also need to apply logical reasoning to describe and compare these cases for common algorithms, such as the searching and sorting algorithms in 2.11.1 and 2.11.2. For example, the best case for a linear search will be achieved when the target item is the first element in the list. Students will not be expected to make reference to Big-O notation. For 2.11.6 students will need to be able to determine which searching algorithm is most appropriate for a given situation. They should consider factors such as whether the data is ordered, the size of the dataset, the need for efficiency, and the ease of implementation. Students will also need to explain the reasoning behind their choice, showing an understanding of the benefits and drawbacks of each algorithm and how these relate to the specific requirements of the task. For 2.11.7 students will need to be able to determine which sorting algorithm is most appropriate for a particular situation. They should consider factors such as the size of the dataset, whether the data is already partially sorted, the importance of speed and memory efficiency, and the complexity of implementation. Students will also need to explain the reasoning for their choice, demonstrating an understanding of the benefits and drawbacks of each sorting algorithm in relation to the task requirements. Content area 2.12 (Testing) For 2.12.1.1 students will need to understand why it is important to test each component of a solution independently before integrating them into the final system. This includes testing software, hardware, data, interfaces and resulting services. Students should also recognise how testing individual components can improve reliability, efficiency, and the overall quality of the final product. For 2.12.2.1 students will need to understand the definition of each testing method (concept, unit, boundary, integration, performance, system, acceptance, usability, regression, load/stress, closed box and open box). For each testing method, students will need to be able to explain its purpose in the development and evaluation of a solution. They should recognise the benefits and drawbacks of each method. For 2.12.2.2 students will need to be able to apply the testing methods listed in 2.12.2.1 to given scenarios. Students should know when it is most appropriate to use them and be able to apply their knowledge to identify suitable scenarios for each type of testing, have an understanding of how different methods contribute to ensuring the reliability, efficiency, usability, and overall quality of a solution. For 2.12.3.1 students will need to understand the automation methods (macros, scripts and functional testing tools) and how they can be used to improve efficiency, accuracy, and consistency in testing and other tasks. They should be able to explain the purpose of each, including the types of tasks each is suitable for and the benefits they provide. Students will also need to recognise situations where automation is appropriate and how it can complement manual testing or other manual processes. For 2.12.4.1 students will need to understand the purpose of test data and the different types of test data (valid, invalid, boundary and erroneous). For each type of test data, students will need to know their purposes in checking the correctness and robustness of a solution and explain why each type is used. Students will also need to recognise how using a variety of test data helps identify errors, ensure the system handles different scenarios correctly, and improve the reliability and quality of the final solution. For 2.12.4.2 students will need to be able to design and create appropriate test data for a given scenario, including valid, invalid, boundary, and erroneous data. They should demonstrate that the test data can be used effectively to check that the solution works as intended and handles a range of input scenarios correctly. For 2.12.4.3 students will need to understand what a test plan is and the purpose it serves in ensuring a solution is thoroughly tested. They should be able to create a test plan and explain each step in a test plan, including identifying the tests to be carried out, describing their purpose, selecting appropriate test data, specifying the expected results, and recording the actual results. Students will also need to understand when a test plan should be used and how it supports systematic, organised, and effective testing of a solution. An example of how 2.12.4.3 could be assessed in core exam paper 1 is shown here: An example of how 2.12.4 could be assessed in the Employer Set Project (Task 2) is shown here: An example of how content area 2 could be assessed in the Employer Set Project (Task 4a) is shown here: Content Area 3 – Emerging issues Content area 3.1 (Impact of Digital Technologies) For 3.1.1 students will need to understand the ways in which greater reliance on digital systems affects both organisations and society. For organisational culture, students should understand the associated impacts of: • Changes in communication methods, such as face to face, email and video calls • Increased productivity and availability expectations • Increase in staff monitoring • New working practices, such as remote, hybrid and in-office working • Automation of services including the use of artificial intelligence (AI) For society, students should understand the associated impacts of: • Loss of jobs • Shift in skill requirements • Reduction in human decision making and loss of empathy • Privacy including digital footprints and surveillance • Changing behaviours, such as loss of social skills and digital identity • Access to wider social networks, including personal and professional • Access to online services, such as government, commercial and entertainment • Potential isolation, including lack of skill, equipment, connectivity and resistance to change • Improved access to information, including professional and personal • Increased use of AI and generative AI, including textual, graphical, video and audio • Globalisation, including access to global media sources Students should be able to describe these effects and understand both positive and negative consequences for different scenarios. For 3.1.2 students will need to understand why digital inclusion is important and how it ensures fair access to digital services for all users. They should be able to explain the need for suitable hardware and software technologies, reliable connectivity, and the importance of checking for bias within datasets. Students should also understand the role of codes of best practice and the key features and purpose of public sector website and mobile application accessibility regulations. They will need to recognise how these measures help make digital services accessible, equitable, and usable by a diverse population. For 3.1.3 students will need to understand how different characteristics of end users can influence how digital systems are used and how inclusive they are. This includes factors such as age, digital skills, literacy levels, whether the user is part of an internal or external audience, and cultural issues, including potential bias in digital systems. Students should also consider additional needs, such as accessibility requirements, and understand how these factors affect design, usability, and overall inclusivity of digital systems. An example of how 3.1.3 could be assessed in core exam paper 1 is shown here: For 3.1.4 students will need to understand how professional development can benefit individuals in the digital industry. This includes increasing industry and sector competence, enhancing employability potential and job security, and providing access to knowledge of, and adherence to, industry standards. Students should be able to explain how engaging in professional improves skills and expertise and helps maintain current knowledge of best practices within the sector. Content area 3.2 (Emerging Technologies) For 3.2.1 students will need to understand the effects of emerging technologies on organisations, individuals, and society as a whole. They should be able to explain impacts related: • Storage media, including the increased demand for storage • Processing technologies, including quantum computing • Internet of Things (IoT), including edge computing and the use within different contexts (industrial, smart city, domestic) • AI, including generative AI and machine learning • Extended reality, including augmented reality and virtual reality • Open source software • Blockchain • Environmental, including consumption of rare metals, energy to produce electronic systems and environmental impact of disposal • Autonomous machines including self-driving cars and robotic assembly lines Students should be able to describe both positive and negative consequences of these technological developments within different scenarios. An example of how 3.2.1 could be assessed in core exam paper 1 is shown here: For 3.2.2 students will need to understand how different digital and emerging technologies interact and influence one another, and how these interrelationships affect organisations, society, and individuals. They should be able to evaluate both positive and negative impacts and make informed judgements about the suitability, risks, and benefits of using these technologies within given situations. Content Area 4 – Legislation and regulatory requirements Content area 4.1 (Legislation) For 4.1.1 students will need to know the responsibilities of, and implications for, employers under relevant health and safety legislation. Students will need to understand the main points of the Health and Safety at Work Act, including the employer’s responsibilities to provide a safe working environment, ensure staff are properly trained, provide adequate welfare, and give relevant information, instruction, and supervision. They should also understand the requirements related to display screen equipment, such as carrying out workstation assessments, reducing risks by encouraging breaks, providing eye tests on request, and offering training and information. For 4.1.2 students will need to understand the health and safety risks associated with working with digital systems, including risks from using display screen equipment and general health and safety hazards. They should also know the preventative measures that can reduce these risks, such as providing adequate training, ensuring a safe working environment, and following safe working practices. Students will need to be able to identify potential risks in different scenarios and explain how these measures help to protect employees. For 4.1.3 students will need to understand the purpose of data security and protection legislation, such as the Data Protection Act and the General Data Protection Regulation. They should be able to explain the eight principles of data protection and understand how these laws affect both organisations and individuals. Students will need to apply this knowledge to recognise how organisations must handle personal data responsibly and the potential consequences of failing to comply with the legislation. For 4.1.4 students will need to understand the principles of the Computer Misuse Act, including the types of offences it covers, such as unauthorised access to systems or data and unauthorised modification of programs or files. They should also understand the consequences of breaching this legislation for both the company and the employee, including legal and disciplinary actions. Students will need to recognise the importance of employee awareness and how organisations can promote safe and lawful use of computer systems. For 4.1.5 students will need to understand equality legislation, including the nine protected characteristics and the different types of discrimination such as direct, indirect, harassment, and victimisation. They should also know the situations in which individuals are protected under the law and understand when and how to take action against discrimination, including awareness of the time limits for making claims. Students will need to be able to explain these concepts and recognise scenarios where equality legislation applies. For 4.1.6 students will need to understand the main types of intellectual property legislation, including unregistered designs, registered designs, and patents. They need to know the purpose of each type of protection, how they apply to creative and technical work. Students will need to recognise situations where intellectual property laws are relevant and the importance of respecting these rights. For 4.1.7 students will need to understand how digital software development interacts with relevant digital legislation, such as data protection, computer misuse, intellectual property, equality, and health and safety laws. They should know how following or breaching these laws can affect organisations, society, and individuals. Students will need to make judgements about the potential impacts, considering both positive outcomes, such as improved security and fairness, and negative consequences, such as legal penalties, financial loss, or harm to individuals. For 4.1.8 students will need to understand that some offences in the digital environment are governed by international law, including laws relating to cyberspace and online activity. They should also understand how international law can apply to surveillance, data access, and cross-border digital crimes. Students will need to be able to explain the relevance of international law and recognise situations where it may affect organisations and individuals. Content area 4.2 (Guidelines) For 4.2.1 students will need to know what is meant by the term code of conduct and the different codes of conduct that exist including organisational codes, professional codes and governmental codes. They should know these specific professional bodies: • British Computer Society (BCS) • The Institution of Analysts and Programmers (IAP) • Chartered Institute of Information Security (CIISec) They should know the purpose of these codes and how they guide professional behaviour. For 4.2.2 students will need to understand how guidelines in codes of conduct influence professional behaviour. They should be able to explain how these guidelines help ensure individuals follow organisational policies, procedures, and legislation, maintain quality of work by minimising risk to the public and acting with competence and integrity, meet deadlines, communicate effectively, and maintain confidentiality and trust. Students will need to be able to apply this understanding to recognise professional behaviours and make judgements about appropriate actions in different workplace scenarios. For 4.2.3 students will need to understand the main sources of digital industry standards including the international bodies: • International Organization for Standardization (ISO) • Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) • World Wide Web Consortium (W3C®) • Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) Students also need to understand the national and sector-specific standards: • British Standards (BS) • Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) • Payment Card Industry Security Standards Council (PCI SSC) Students should know the purpose of these standards and how they guide best practice, quality, security, and accessibility in digital systems. For 4.2.4 students will need to understand the purpose of AUPs, and how they aim to set clear rules for the responsible use of digital systems within an organisation. They should know the typical content of an AUP, including permitted and prohibited activities, working practices such as maintaining confidentiality, communication etiquette to ensure the organisation’s image is upheld, and the sanctions or penalties for breaching the policy. Students will need to recognise how AUPs guide employee behaviour and protect both individuals and the organisation.
